title: SPATIAL AND SOCIAL ASPECTS OF CROWDING PERCEPTION
research_question: This study examined the effects of room color and visual complexity on perceptions of room capacity and judgments of crowding, mediated by social orientation.

participants.description: Eighty male and female undergraduates at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. More than 80% were raised in Metropolitan New York, with similar ages and family histories.
participants.recruitment: Received partial course credit in Introductory Psychology as compensation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four scale model rooms (20.5 feet square, 8.5 feet high at 1:18 scale) constructed of plywood with cork floors. Two rooms were painted light green (Sears No. 0866), and two dark green (Sears No. 0872). Two rooms had low visual complexity (devoid of features), and two had high visual complexity (pictures on two walls: a 2.5x2.5 inch graphic lion, a 2.5x2.5 inch bridge painting, and a 1.5x2.5 inch city street picture). Small clothespin figures (3.5 inches tall, representing 5'8" people) were used.

measures.instrument: Number of clothespin figures placed until 'you begin to feel crowded.'
Location of the figure representing the subject (right half near pictures vs. other)
Questionnaire (age, sex, SAT scores, ordinal position, family size, residential history)

findings.antecedent: Room color (light green vs. dark green)
findings.consequent: Number of figures placed (perceived room capacity)
findings.mechanism: Light colors cause interiors to appear larger, increasing the amount of space perceived as available, thus increasing the threshold for crowding.
findings.quote: color differences accounted for a significant amount of the variance in the number of figures placed in each room (F = 25.116, p < .001): more figures were placed in the light green rooms than in the dark green rooms
effect_size_assumptions: Direction is unknown from p-value alone; returned d is magnitude only.

findings.consequent: Number of figures placed (perceived room capacity)
findings.quote: the visual complexity variable did not account for a significant share of the variance (F = .836, p > .3)

findings.consequent: Number of figures placed (perceived room capacity)
findings.quote: the effect of orientation reported by Desor was not obtained (F = .482, p > .4).

findings.antecedent: Interaction of orientation (social vs. nonsocial) and room color (light green vs. dark green) in high visual complexity rooms
findings.consequent: Number of figures placed (perceived room capacity)
findings.mechanism: In nonsocial dark, high complexity rooms, additional nonsocial stimulation combined with limited perceived space may lead to sensory overload, reducing capacity. In social dark, high complexity rooms, complexity provides alternative loci for attention, reducing social stimulation.
findings.quote: When the high complexity conditions were considered alone, the interaction of orientation and room color approached significance (F = 2.72, p = .1)

findings.mechanism: Subjects may be using the alternative interaction loci provided by increased complexity to avoid social contact by attending to nonsocial elements.
findings.quote: those considering high complexity rooms tended to place themselves in the right half near the pictures (X2 = 6.084, df = 1, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Dark green, high visual complexity room under nonsocial orientation
findings.mechanism: In nonsocial settings, visual complexity might add to nonsocial stimulation, leading to sensory overload rather than providing a distraction from social interaction.
findings.quote: Self-placement in the right half of the dark, high complexity room considered under nonsocial conditions was considerably lower than in the other rooms characterized by high visual complexity.

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Dark colors result in perceptions of decreased spatial availability.
findings.quote: dark green rooms rated them significantly smaller than those rating light green rooms (F = 26.259, p < .001).

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The combination of dark color (limiting perceived space) and additional nonsocial stimulation from visual complexity in a nonsocial context may lead to sensory overload and reduced perceived size.
findings.quote: the dark green room characterized by high visual complexity was perceived as smaller than other high complexity rooms when considered under a nonsocial orientation (F = 15.003, p < .001).

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Dark colors result in perceptions of decreased spatial availability, which may contribute to feelings of stuffiness.

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The three-way interaction suggests that the effect of color on stuffiness is modulated by complexity and orientation, similar to perceived room size.
findings.quote: showed the same three-way interactions as did ratings of room size (F = 5.389, p < .05 and F = 5.816, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Dark colors result in perceptions of decreased spatial availability, lowering the threshold for crowding.
findings.quote: the degree to which crowding was perceived in the rooms (F = 10.544, p < .01)

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The three-way interaction suggests that the effect of color on crowdedness is modulated by complexity and orientation, similar to perceived room size.
findings.quote: showed the same three-way interactions as did ratings of room size (F = 5.389, p < .05 and F = 5.816, p < .05).
female subjects indicated that they liked the rooms more than males did (F = 7.031, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Room color, visual complexity, social orientation
findings.quote: The absence of any effects of room color, visual complexity, or social orientation on the ratings of prettiness and attraction indicated that these manipulations did not alter aesthetic ratings of the rooms or influence preference for them.

findings.antecedent: Personal characteristics (age, family size, ordinal position, residential history)
findings.mechanism: The sample's homogeneity likely limited the possibility of observing differences along these dimensions.
findings.quote: Personal characteristics... were not related to any of the dependent variables; correlations for these relationships did not exceed .25.

mechanisms: Light colors cause interiors to appear larger, increasing the amount of space perceived as available, thus increasing the threshold for crowding.
Dark colors result in perceptions of decreased spatial availability, lowering the threshold for crowding.
Visual complexity provides alternative behaviors (loci for attention) to divert attention from social stimulation, reducing its impact in social settings.
In nonsocial settings, visual complexity, especially combined with dark colors, may add to nonsocial stimulation, leading to sensory overload and reduced perceived room capacity.
implementation_implications: By varying color, designers can increase the number of individuals who may comfortably interact in an interior space.

Design decisions should consider as many elements of a setting as possible, as perceptions of crowding and room capacity are influenced by the juxtaposition of environmental elements and psychological characteristics of users.

limitations: Generalizability is limited as subjects in model-room studies do not have real experience in the setting.

Visual properties assume artificial importance due to the absence of other forms of stimulation (olfactory, tactile, direct interaction demands), potentially exaggerating the importance of visual cues.
The experience of crowding as an interpersonal process was hindered by the artificial limitations of interaction in model rooms.
Findings should be considered with caution until replicated and extended in actual settings with complete and unlimited interpersonal interaction.
Failure to replicate Desor's findings on social orientation may be due to using only two of her four activity types.

The sample was relatively homogeneous (mostly from Metropolitan New York, similar ages and family histories), which may have limited the possibility of observing differences along background dimensions.

mechanism_chain.description: Room color influences the perceived spaciousness or openness of a room, which in turn affects an individual's judgment of how many people or figures can comfortably fit into that space.

instruments_used.name: Capacity Estimation Task
instruments_used.description: Participants were asked to indicate the maximum number of figures or people that could comfortably fit into a given room.
